positions.stance: Opposes longer commutes, crowded schools, higher costs, and fewer choices from growth; would ensure a person working 40 hours a week can afford housing, groceries, utilities, childcare, and healthcare; supports teachers, nurses, first responders, young families, and retirees being able to afford a home in their own communities.

positions.stance: Opposes giving blank checks to projects that eliminate jobs, expand surveillance, or send benefits elsewhere, supports long-term investment in people, communities, opportunity, and infrastructure, believes Georgia's economy should reward hard work, not only wealth and political connections, and supports building good jobs in healthcare, solar, and skilled trades tied to local training.

Prepare Georgia for the next generation with long-term investment in people, communities, opportunity, and the infrastructure to support them.

positions.stance: Supports lower everyday costs, living wages, affordable homes, and taxes that work for regular people, opposes subsidizing major employers that pay poverty wages, and supports lower taxes for people in District 31 and opposes schemes that shift burdens onto homeowners.
q: Lower everyday costs, living wages, affordable homes, and taxes that work for regular people.
Taxpayers should not subsidize major employers that pay poverty wages.

positions.stance: Supports honest prices, fair contracts, safe products, and control over personal information, supports lower costs, better jobs, consumer protections, and accountable corporate citizenship, and believes government should help people have more time, more security, and a fair shot at a good life.

Lower costs, better jobs, consumer protections, and accountable corporate citizenship belong together.

positions.stance: Believes Georgia should trust adults, protect rights, and make democratic participation easier, believes adults should be free to make decisions about their bodies, families, beliefs, and private lives, and believes government should protect rights, not micromanage them.

Adults should be free to make decisions about their bodies, families, beliefs, and private lives, so long as they are not harming others.

positions.stance: Would ensure anyone working full time earns enough for food, housing, healthcare, transportation and a little breathing room, supports a full-time job being enough to build a stable life.
q: Anyone working full time should earn enough for food, housing, healthcare, transportation, and a little breathing room.
A full-time job ought to be enough to build a stable life.

positions.stance: Supports learning primarily happening in the classroom, leaving room for family, play, rest, and creativity after the bell.
q: Learning should primarily happen in the classroom, leaving room for family, play, rest, and creativity after the bell.
Kids already spend most of the day in school. Learning should primarily happen in the classroom, leaving room for family, play, rest, and creativity after the bell.

positions.stance: Supports healthcare being a basic right, not a profit center, with accessible and affordable care.
q: Healthcare should be a basic right, not a profit center.
Healthcare should be a basic right, not a profit center. Georgia can build a system that puts patients first and makes care — including mental-health care — accessible and affordable.

positions.stance: Supports awareness of data centers' demands on land, power, water, and local infrastructure, opposes data centers that eliminate jobs and expand surveillance without public benefit.

positions.stance: Supports voters choosing their representatives and ending partisan gerrymandering, believes political maps should reflect real communities and the people who live in them.
q: Voters should choose their representatives — not the other way around. Political maps should reflect real communities and the people who live in them, not protect politicians or silence voters. End partisan gerrymandering and draw fair districts the public can trust.
Political maps should reflect real communities and the people who live in them, not protect politicians or silence voters.

positions.stance: Believes growth should be planned with jobs, infrastructure, and accountable government, supports better roads, smarter planning, and real transit options for people to get to work.

Match District 31’s growth with better roads, smarter planning, and real transit options so people can get to work without spending their lives behind the wheel.

BARRY LOUDERMILK.name: Barry Loudermilk
BARRY LOUDERMILK.background: U.S. Representative for Georgia's 11th District since Jan. 3, 2015 (Republican); did not seek re-election in 2026. Born Dec. 22, 1963, in Riverdale, Ga. U.S. Air Force communications operations specialist, 1984-1992; A.A.S. telecommunications technology, Community College of the Air Force (1987); B.S., Wayland Baptist University (1992). Founded the IT firm Innovative Network Systems, Inc. and co-owned the Freedom Flight Center. Chairman, Bartow County Republican Party, 2001-2004; Georgia House of Representatives (District 14), 2005-2010; Georgia State Senate (District 52, then 14), 2011-Aug. 2013, resigning to run for Congress. Baptist; three children.
BARRY LOUDERMILK.ideology: Describes himself as a 'constitutional conservative.' A former House Freedom Caucus member who left the group in 2017 citing lack of time and became more active in the Republican Study Committee (Almanac of American Politics, via Wikipedia); Heritage Action scored him 84% in the 114th Congress versus 63% for the average House Republican, and Club for Growth called him a 'defender of economic freedom' (2016). Endorsed by President Trump for 2026 before he retired; one of 139 House Republicans who voted to reject electoral votes from Arizona and Pennsylvania on Jan. 6-7, 2021.
BARRY LOUDERMILK.record: Six-term congressman (2015-2027). Cast one of three votes against John Boehner for Speaker in Jan. 2015. Committees: Financial Services (vice chair of the Financial Institutions and Monetary Policy subcommittee, 2023-24), House Administration (Elections subcommittee; Oversight subcommittee chair as of Dec. 2024), Joint Committee on the Library; earlier Homeland Security and Science, Space and Technology (Oversight subcommittee chair, 2015-16). Led a Jan. 5, 2021 Capitol-complex tour that the House Jan. 6 Select Committee questioned in 2022; Capitol Police Chief Tom Manger said there was no evidence he entered the Capitol with the group or that the tour was suspicious; he filed an ethics complaint against members who called it a reconnaissance tour. In 2017 introduced an Equifax-related bill capping class-action damages at $500,000, then agreed to delay it after criticism (he had received $2,000 from Equifax). Chaired the House Judiciary select subcommittee on Jan. 6 from Jan. 2025. In July 2026 the House passed his bill naming the Cobb VA clinic for Col. Mike Boyce and the Main Street Capital Access Act (H.R. 6955) containing two of his provisions. Announced in Feb. 2026 (AJC, Feb. 4, 2026) that he would not seek re-election; John Cowan (R) won the seat in Nov. 2026.

Campaign finance by cycle not captured. Wikipedia says 52nd then 14th after 2013 redistricting). Loudermilk is listed as a withdrawn 2026 GA-11 candidate; he retired and John Cowan (R) won the seat Nov. 3, 2026.
